# Data import and inspection {#sec-datenimport}

```{r setup-kap4, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(mariposa)
source("R/_common_en.R")
```

> *Who holds Islamophobic attitudes in Germany in 2023?*

Before you can answer this question, you need the dataset on your computer, and you need to understand it well enough to pick out the right variables. This chapter takes you from importing the SPSS file through the first inspection steps to handling missing values properly. In @sec-datentransformation you then build the two scales of the mini study on this basis.

::: {.callout-note}
**Research journal: Where are you in your mini study?** Your tools are set up (Chapters 1–3). Now the actual research work begins. At the end of this chapter you have an analysis dataset: 5246 respondents, your own set of variables, missing values declared. This is the raw state on which all further stages build.
:::

## What this chapter is about

Imagine a colleague gives you a USB stick labelled *“ALLBUS 2023, have fun”*. You plug it in and open the file. What you see is not what you hoped for: 579 columns with names such as `mm01`, `pa29`, `pt06`, `wghtpew`. Negative numbers appear where you would expect answers: `-8`, `-9`, `-11`, `-42` and a dozen or so more. Some variables are stored as numbers although they are really categories (`sex = 1` means “male”). And the actual labels, the wording of what was asked, are hidden somewhere in the background.

This is normal. Secondary datasets in quantitative social research always look like this. They are built so that many people can use them for many different questions, and that only works if the data stay raw at first. Your task is to turn this raw state into an analysis dataset that fits your research question.

Take your time over these steps. They are the methodological core of any honest analysis: Which cases do you exclude? How do you handle missing values? How do you translate `mm01 = 7` into “this person strongly rejects Muslims”? Each of these decisions affects the result, and each belongs in a pipeline that you can reproduce at any time, as open science requires.

Everything that follows builds on this chapter. Here you create the analysis dataset that you use to describe distributions in @sec-univbivar, check structures in @sec-latente and model hypotheses in @sec-erklaerung. Any error made here affects all later findings.

## What you will be able to do after this chapter {-}

- Import an SPSS dataset with `read_spss()`, including all variable and value labels.
- Search for variables by name or label with `find_var()`.
- Create detailed codebooks for selected variables with `codebook()`.
- Select, filter, sort and reorder variables and cases (`select()`, `filter()`, `arrange()`, `relocate()`).
- Understand the `<haven_labelled>` data type and convert it to a factor or a number when needed.
- Read, extract and set variable labels and value labels.
- Declare missing values and handle them systematically with `na_frequencies()`, `set_na()` and `drop_na()`.

## Setup

In every R session, you first load the packages you work with. Throughout this book there are only two:

```{r setup-show, eval=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(mariposa)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
**SPSS → R: Loading packages.** In SPSS, all functions are available straight away. In R, you use `library()` to activate the tools you need. This keeps the set of function names manageable and makes each step traceable.
:::

## Importing the dataset with `read_spss()`

The 2023 German General Social Survey (ALLBUS) is stored in your project folder as an SPSS file (`ALLBUS2023.sav`). You import it with `read_spss()` from mariposa. The English edition of the dataset stores the codes for missing values (“no answer”, “don't know”, “not applicable” and others) as ordinary numbers, so you declare them as missing when you read the file. `set_na()` without a variable name applies the codes to all numeric variables; @sec-fehlende-werte explains `set_na()`.

```{r read-allbus}
allbus <- read_spss("ALLBUS2023.sav") |>
  set_na(-56, -55, -54, -53, -51, -50, -42, -41,
         -33, -32, -15, -11, -10, -9, -8, -7, -6)
```

`allbus` is now a tibble, a modern data type in the tidyverse. Tibbles behave like classic data frames, but they print more compactly and keep their column types more reliably. This is what you have loaded:

```{r read-show}
allbus
```

The header shows `5,246 × 579`: the dataset has 5246 cases and 579 variables. Below it you see a selection of the first columns with their data types.

@fig-einlesen shows the path from the file to the object: `read_spss()` reads `ALLBUS2023.sav` from the project folder, and the result is stored under the name `allbus`. From now on you work with this object in R; the file on your hard drive stays unchanged.

![`read_spss()` reads the SPSS file, `set_na()` turns the missing-value codes into `NA`, and the result is stored as the object `allbus`.](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-einlesen.svg){#fig-einlesen .lightbox fig-alt="On the left a file tile ALLBUS2023.sav, labelled File in the project folder. An arrow leads to a green box read_spss(), labelled Function from mariposa. Another arrow leads to a baseplate with towers of blue and purple bricks under the dark name tag allbus, next to it 5,246 × 579, labelled Object in R. Below, the code as bricks on two lines: allbus <- read_spss(“ALLBUS2023.sav”) and, on the next line, |> set_na(-56, …, -6). allbus is dark, read_spss and set_na are green, the file name and the codes are orange."}

What do the small type markers under each column mean? Directly below each column name, the tibble prints a type tag in angle brackets. Here is a short glossary:

| Tag           | Meaning                            | Example                           |
| :------------ | :--------------------------------- | :-------------------------------- |
| `<int>`       | whole number (integer)             | case ID, count                    |
| `<dbl>`       | decimal number (double)            | age, scale mean                   |
| `<chr>`       | text (character)                   | variable with text responses      |
| `<fct>`       | factor (category with levels)      | recoded education levels          |
| `<dbl+lbl>`   | labelled double from SPSS          | typical ALLBUS variable           |
| `<lgl>`       | logical (`TRUE`/`FALSE`)           | result of a condition             |

You will see the `<dbl+lbl>` type everywhere in ALLBUS. It is created when you import the file. In the background, `read_spss()` uses the `haven` package and adds two properties you know from SPSS: **variable labels** (a descriptive label for each column) and **value labels** (a label for each value). Both are stored in the columns without being visible; you can retrieve them at any time or make them visible as a factor.

Most variables therefore arrive as `<haven_labelled>` columns, printed as `<dbl+lbl>`. Such a column is not a factor. The values stay numeric, so you can still calculate with them, and in the background they keep their SPSS value labels (“1 = MALE, 2 = FEMALE, …”). For example:

```{r labelled-demo}
allbus$sex |> head(5)
```

At the top are the variable label and the first five values, below them the table of labels. The rows `NA(g)` and `NA(n)` are the variable's missing codes. More on these in @sec-fehlende-werte.

Three operations are common:

- Calculate with the variable (`mean(allbus$sex, na.rm = TRUE)`) → works directly, but usually gives meaningless values for categorical variables.
- Make it readable for plots (`allbus |> to_label(sex)`) → converts it into a factor with the labels as levels.
- Keep the plain number (`allbus |> to_numeric(sex)`) → removes the label layer.

The details follow in @sec-datentypen-verstehen.

### Other formats and export with `read_stata()`, `read_xlsx()` and `write_spss()`

If you need data in other formats, there are matching functions:

```{r read-formats, eval=FALSE}
read_stata("file.dta")     # Stata
read_sas("file.sas7bdat")  # SAS
read_xlsx("file.xlsx")     # Excel
```

And if you want to export an edited dataset back to SPSS:

```{r write-spss, eval=FALSE}
write_spss(allbus, "allbus_edited.sav")
```

## A first look at the dataset with `glimpse()`, `nrow()` and `ncol()`

With almost 600 variables, you cannot display everything in the console. Three tools help you find your way around:

```{r first-look, results='hide'}
glimpse(allbus)           # compact overview of the structure
nrow(allbus)              # number of cases
ncol(allbus)              # number of variables
```

`nrow()` returns 5246 and `ncol()` returns 579. So `allbus` is a baseplate with 5246 rows and 579 towers (@fig-platte): each row is a respondent, each tower a variable. An empty brick means that there is no valid value for this person on this variable.

![A section of `allbus`: the first five rows of the variables `respid`, `age` and `mm01`. For `mm01`, the value is missing in three rows.](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-platte.svg){#fig-platte .lightbox fig-alt="Baseplate with the name tag allbus and three towers respid, age and mm01, next to them an ellipsis for further towers. respid shows 1 to 5, age 50, 51, 69, 72 and 18, mm01 the value 5, three empty dashed bricks and 2. The first row is outlined in orange, the tower age in green. On the right three boxes: A row is a case, nrow(allbus) gives [1] 5246. A tower is a variable, ncol(allbus) gives [1] 579. An empty brick is a missing value."}

### Finding variables with `find_var()`

The variable names in ALLBUS are cryptic (`mm01`, `pa29`, `wghtpew`). What is actually measured is given in the variable label. mariposa's `find_var()` searches both at the same time, name and label, and returns the matches as a small table:

```{r find-var-demo}
allbus |> find_var("muslim")
```

For each match, the table shows the position of the variable in the dataset (`col`), its name and the full label; the search is not case-sensitive. There are six matches: five of the six items of our scale and `ma08`. The item `mm02` refers to “Islam” rather than “Muslims”. Because the search pattern is a **regular expression**, you can search for both terms at once; `|` means “or”:

```{r find-var-regex}
allbus |> find_var("islam|muslim")
```

Now all six `mm` items for our Islamophobia scale are together (plus `ma08`, an item on religious instruction for Muslims in schools from a different question block). If, on the other hand, you are searching literally for characters that have a special meaning in regular expressions (such as the full stop in `RELIG.`), set `fixed = TRUE`. By default, `find_var()` searches names and labels; with `search = "label"` you restrict the search to labels, with `search = "name"` to names:

```{r find-var-labels}
allbus |> find_var("age", search = "label")
allbus |> find_var("^mm", search = "name")     # regex: all mm items
```

### Detailed overview with `codebook()`

For a specific selection of variables, `codebook()` from mariposa produces an HTML overview with labels, values and frequencies. It is the R equivalent of `DISPLAY DICTIONARY` in SPSS:

```{r codebook}
allbus |>
  codebook(mm01, mm02, mm03, mm04, mm05, mm06)
```

In RStudio, the overview opens in the Viewer tab; in a Quarto document such as this book, mariposa embeds it directly in the report. To pass it on, save it as a separate HTML file with `codebook(..., file = "codebook.html")` or as an Excel spreadsheet with `write_xlsx(codebook(...), "codebook.xlsx")`.

In a methods section, each scale needs a short codebook: item wording, response format, treatment of missing values, N per item. If you create this codebook with `codebook()` and put it in the appendix of your report, you meet this requirement.

::: {.callout-tip}
**SPSS → R: Inspecting data.** In SPSS, you use `DISPLAY DICTIONARY` for a complete overview. `find_var()` is more targeted: you search for a keyword and immediately get the matching variables, even if you do not remember the cryptic names.

| SPSS                            | R                                |
| ------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `FREQUENCIES VARIABLES=mm01.`   | `allbus |> frequency(mm01)`      |
| `DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=age.`   | `allbus |> describe(age)`        |
| `DISPLAY DICTIONARY.`           | `allbus |> codebook(...)`        |
:::

## Selecting variables and cases

The `dplyr` functions `select()`, `filter()` and `arrange()` are the tools you use every day to take what you need from a large dataset.

### Selecting variables with `select()`

```{r select-basic}
allbus |>
  select(mm01, mm02, mm03)
```

`select()` keeps only the towers you name; all 5246 rows stay on the baseplate (@fig-select).

![`select(mm01, mm02, mm03)` keeps three towers. The towers that are dropped are grey; the number of rows stays at 5246.](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-select.svg){#fig-select .lightbox fig-alt="On the left the baseplate allbus, 5,246 × 579, with the towers respid, mm01, mm02, mm03 and mm04 and an ellipsis for further towers; the first five rows are shown. respid and mm04 are grey. mm01 to mm03 show 5, 3 and 4 at the top and 2, 4 and 4 at the bottom, with three empty bricks in between. A green arrow select() leads to a new baseplate, 5,246 × 3, with only the towers mm01, mm02 and mm03. Below, the code allbus |> select(mm01, mm02, mm03)."}

You can specify ranges with `:` and exclude variables with `-`:

```{r select-range}
allbus |>
  select(mm01:mm06, eastwest, sex, age, educ)
```

This selection, the six scale items plus demographics, is what you need for the mini study.

In @sec-datentypen you extracted a single column with `$`. You can also do this with `select()`, but you get a different object back:

```{r dollar-select}
allbus$age |> head(5)
allbus |> select(age) |> head(5)
```

`allbus$age` returns a vector: the five numbers after `[1]`, with the table of labels below. `allbus |> select(age)` returns a tibble with one column. On the left, @fig-dollar-select shows a single tower, on the right a baseplate with one tower. Which form you need depends on the next function: functions that calculate, such as `mean()`, expect a vector; dplyr functions such as `filter()` expect a dataset.

![On the left, `$` returns the values of `age` as a vector; on the right, `select()` returns a tibble with the column `age`. Both contain the same five values.](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-dollar-select.svg){#fig-dollar-select .lightbox fig-alt="Two halves. On the left the code allbus$age |> head(5), below it a tower of five blue bricks 50, 51, 69, 72 and 18 on a short base, labelled Vector, next to it the output [1] 50 51 69 72 18. On the right the code allbus |> select(age) |> head(5), below it the dimensions 5 × 1 and the same tower with the column header age and the type dbl+lbl on a wide baseplate with room for further towers, labelled Tibble."}

**Stop and think.** What does `allbus |> select(age) |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)` return?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
```{r dollar-select-loesung}
#| warning: true
allbus |> select(age) |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)
mean(allbus$age, na.rm = TRUE)
```

In the first call, `mean()` receives a baseplate instead of a tower. It cannot calculate with that: R issues a warning and returns `NA`. In the second call, `mean()` receives the tower `allbus$age` and calculates the mean age, about 52.5 years. In a pipe, you take the tower out with `pull(age)`.
:::

#### Tidyselect helpers such as `starts_with()`, `where()` and `everything()`

With large datasets such as ALLBUS, you often want to select all variables that match a pattern. Instead of listing them one by one, you can use the following functions:

| Helper                  | Effect                                               | Example with ALLBUS                     |
| :---------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------- |
| `starts_with("pre")`    | all variables whose name starts with `pre`           | `select(starts_with("mm0"))`            |
| `ends_with("suffix")`   | all variables whose name ends with `suffix`          | `select(ends_with("educ"))`: school-leaving certificate of respondent, partner and parents |
| `contains("part")`      | all variables whose name contains `part`             | `select(contains("wght"))`: the four weighting variables |
| `matches("regex")`      | all variables that match the regular expression      | `select(matches("^p[at]"))`             |
| `where(is.numeric)`     | all variables whose content meets a condition        | `select(where(is.numeric))`             |
| `everything()`          | all remaining variables, typically in `relocate()`   | `relocate(respid, .before = everything())` |

These helpers work in the same way in `mutate(across(...))`, `summarise(across(...))` and in many mariposa functions. They are part of a vocabulary shared across the tidyverse.

#### Extracting and reordering columns with `pull()` and `relocate()`

Two close relatives of `select()`:

- `pull(var)` extracts a single column as a plain vector. This is useful when you want to pass the content of the column directly to a function that does not expect a tibble: `allbus |> pull(age) |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)`.
- `relocate(var, .before = X, .after = Y)` reorders columns without removing any. This is handy when you want the most important variables at the front: `allbus |> relocate(mm01:mm06, eastwest, sex, age, educ, .before = everything())`.

### Filtering cases with `filter()`

```{r filter-basic}
allbus |>
  filter(sex == 2) |>
  select(sex, age, educ)
```

`filter()` checks the condition `sex == 2` for each row and keeps only the rows in which it is true. Code 2 stands for FEMALE; 2672 respondents remain (@fig-filter). `select()` then keeps the three columns.

![`filter(sex == 2)` keeps only the rows with code 2 (FEMALE). The rows that are dropped are grey; the first six rows are shown.](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-filter.svg){#fig-filter .lightbox fig-alt="On the left the baseplate allbus, 5,246 × 579, with the towers sex, age and educ and an ellipsis for further towers; the first six rows are shown. The bricks of sex carry stickers: 1 MALE, 1 MALE, 2 FEMALE, 1 MALE, 2 FEMALE, 2 FEMALE. The three MALE rows with the ages 50, 51 and 72 are grey. A green arrow with sex == 2 leads to a new baseplate, 2,672 × 3, with the three FEMALE rows: ages 69, 18 and 45, educ 4, 5 and 5, below them an ellipsis. Below, the code allbus |> filter(sex == 2) |> select(sex, age, educ)."}

The comparison and logical operators from @sec-operatoren (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `&`, `|`, `%in%`) are your vocabulary here. You can combine them freely into more complex filters:

```{r filter-complex}
allbus |>
  filter(eastwest == 2 & age >= 30 & age <= 60) |>
  select(eastwest, age, educ) |>
  nrow()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**Caution: Missing values.** `filter()` automatically excludes cases with `NA` in the condition. This is usually what you want, but it can take you by surprise. Compare three variants:

```{r filter-na-trio, eval=FALSE}
allbus |> filter(sex == 1)        # men only (NAs are excluded)
allbus |> filter(is.na(sex))      # only cases where sex is missing
allbus |> filter(!is.na(sex))     # all cases where sex is present
```

`sex == 1` compares each row separately (@fig-filter-na). In row 110, `sex` is missing (NO ANSWER). R cannot tell whether this value is 1, so the comparison also gives `NA`. `filter()` keeps only the rows with `TRUE`, so row 110 is dropped in the same way as the row with `FALSE`. `is.na(sex)` only asks whether the value is missing, and it always gives `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

![`filter(sex == 1)` keeps only the rows in which the comparison gives `TRUE`. Where `sex` is missing, the result of the comparison is also an empty brick, and the row is dropped.](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-filter-na.svg){#fig-filter-na .lightbox fig-alt="On the left the tower sex, dbl+lbl, with the rows 1, 2, 3 and 110: 1 MALE, 1 MALE, 2 FEMALE in grey, an ellipsis and an empty dashed brick with the faded sticker NO ANSWER. Next to it the pink tower sex == 1 with TRUE, TRUE, FALSE and an empty dashed brick NA. A green arrow filter() leads to the tower sex with two bricks 1 MALE at the height of rows 1 and 2, below them an ellipsis. Below, the code allbus |> filter(sex == 1)."}

If your number of cases is suddenly smaller than you expected, the `NA` filtering is usually the reason.
:::

**Stop and think.** `allbus |> filter(sex == 1)` keeps 2546 rows, `filter(sex == 2)` keeps 2672 (@fig-filter). Together that makes 5218, but `allbus` has 5246 rows. Where are the other 28?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
```{r filter-na-loesung}
allbus |> frequency(sex)
```

Eighteen respondents have code 3 (NON-BINARY) on `sex`; neither `sex == 1` nor `sex == 2` includes them. For the other 10, the value is missing (NO ANSWER nine times, DATA ERROR: MR once), and these rows are dropped by every comparison with `==`. `filter(is.na(sex))` gives you exactly these 10 rows.
:::

### Sorting cases with `arrange()` and `desc()`

```{r arrange}
allbus |>
  select(age, educ) |>
  arrange(age) |>
  head(5)
```

In descending order with `desc()`:

```{r arrange-desc}
allbus |>
  select(age, educ) |>
  arrange(desc(age)) |>
  head(5)
```

## Understanding data types with `class()` {#sec-datentypen-verstehen}

When you work in SPSS, you rarely ask yourself which type a variable is. SPSS handles this in the background: a variable is “numeric” or “string”, and value labels (“1 = male, 2 = female”) are just a layer of labels on top. In R, this works a little differently, which can be confusing at first.

R has a number of data types: plain numbers (`numeric`), text (`character`), logical values (`logical`) and categories with a fixed order (`factor`). When you import an SPSS dataset, there is one more type, which mariposa adopts from the haven package: `<haven_labelled>`. It is a kind of hybrid: the column behaves like a number, but in the background the values keep their SPSS value labels. This way the information “1 means male” is kept, and you do not have to look it up in the codebook.

`class()` shows you the type of a variable:

```{r class-show}
class(allbus$sex)
class(allbus$age)
```

Both variables are `double`, that is, numbers, and at the same time `haven_labelled`. So a value of `sex` is a brick with a sticker, for example the number 1 with the value label MALE (@fig-dbl-lbl). The tibble shows this as the type tag `<dbl+lbl>`. For `age`, only the missing code has a label; that is enough to make the variable labelled.

![A value of `sex`: the number 1 with the sticker MALE. `dbl` stands for the number (`double`), `lbl` for the value label (`haven_labelled`).](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-dbl-lbl.svg){#fig-dbl-lbl .lightbox fig-alt="At the top sex and the type tag dbl+lbl in angle brackets, dbl dark blue, lbl orange. Below, a large blue brick with the number 1 and a yellow sticker MALE. Under the number it says Number and double, under the sticker Value label and haven_labelled. On the right the code class(allbus$sex) with the output [1] “haven_labelled” “vctrs_vctr” “double”."}

### Converting labelled variables with `to_label()`, `to_numeric()` and `unlabel()`

You will need three conversions again and again:

| Function                              | Effect                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `to_label(data, var)`                 | converts `<haven_labelled>` into a factor with the value labels as levels; the usual choice when you want readable labels on `ggplot()` axes |
| `to_numeric(data, var)`               | converts into a plain numeric vector; the labels are lost                                                                      |
| `to_labelled(data, var, labels = ...)`| converts a factor back into a `<haven_labelled>`                                                                               |

```{r to-label}
allbus |>
  to_label(sex, eastwest) |>
  select(sex, eastwest) |>
  head(3)
```

`to_label()` turns the sticker into the value: the 1 with the label MALE becomes the factor level `MALE` (@fig-to-label). `to_numeric()` peels off the sticker and leaves the number 1.

![The first three values of `sex` before and after conversion. `to_label()` gives a factor with the labels as values, `to_numeric()` gives the numbers without labels.](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-to-label.svg){#fig-to-label .lightbox fig-alt="On the left the tower sex, dbl+lbl, with three blue bricks 1, 1 and 2 and the yellow stickers MALE, MALE and FEMALE. A fork leads with to_label() to a purple tower sex, fct, with MALE, MALE and FEMALE, labelled Factor, and with to_numeric() to a blue tower sex, dbl, with 1, 1 and 2, labelled Number without label."}

If you only want to strip off the labels (for example because a function cannot handle labelled vectors), use `unlabel()`: `allbus |> unlabel(sex, age)`. You will rarely need it, but it is useful when another package will not accept labelled vectors.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Background: Why not just use a factor?

In SPSS, variables are either numeric or string. Value labels are an add-on. In R, factors (categories) and numeric vectors are separate types. `<haven_labelled>` is a bridge: you work with numbers, but the value labels travel with them. When to convert:

- `to_label()` when you sort, group, cross-tabulate or plot; factors give readable output.
- `to_numeric()` when you calculate or build scales, for example with Likert items that you treat as quasi-interval.
- Keep the original if the variable is not final yet and you will need the labels later.
:::

## Reading and setting variable and value labels with `var_label()` and `val_labels()`

| Function                                            | Effect                                                               |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `var_label(data)`                                   | read variable labels                                                 |
| `var_label(data$var) <- "New label"`                | set the variable label of one column                                 |
| `var_label(data) <- list(var = "New label")`        | set the variable labels of several columns at once                   |
| `val_labels(data)`                                  | read value labels                                                    |
| `data <- val_labels(data, var = c("value label 1" = 1, "value label 2" = 2))` | set value labels |
| `data <- val_labels(data, var = c("value label 1" = 1), .add = TRUE)` | change or add individual value labels and keep the others |
| `drop_labels(data)`                                | remove all value labels whose value does not occur in the data       |

```{r labels-read}
allbus |>
  select(mm01, mm02, mm03) |>
  var_label()
```

The result is a named character vector with the stored label for each variable. This tells you what a cryptic variable such as `mm01` means, so you do not have to look it up in the codebook.

A variable such as `mm01` carries three labels (@fig-labels): the variable name you work with in R, the variable label that `var_label()` reads, and the value labels that say what a number means. For `mm01`, only the end points 1 and 7 have a value label; for 2 to 6, `val_labels()` shows only `..`.

![The three labels of `mm01`: variable name, variable label and value labels. The value labels are stuck to the bricks as stickers.](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-labels.svg){#fig-labels .lightbox fig-alt="Three rows. First row: a dark name tag mm01, on the right Variable name. Second row: the text “EXERCISE OF MUSLIM FAITH SHLD BE LIMITED”, on the right Variable label and var_label(). Third row: a blue brick 1 with the sticker COMPLETELY DISAGREE, an ellipsis and a blue brick 7 with the sticker COMPLETELY AGREE, on the right Value labels and val_labels()."}

When you create a new variable (for example a scale in @sec-datentransformation), you can give it a descriptive label afterwards:

```{r label-set, eval=FALSE}
var_label(allbus$islamophobia) <- "Islamophobia scale (6 items, 1–7)"
```

This label then appears automatically in `codebook()`, in the header of `frequency()` and in many `summary()` outputs, wherever mariposa looks for labels. For several variables at once, you pass a list: `var_label(allbus) <- list(islamophobia = "…", populism = "…")`.

Value labels are not set with an arrow on the column. `val_labels()` takes pairs of a variable and a named vector (`"Label" = code`) and returns the changed dataset, which you assign back to `allbus`. A typical case: a 0/1 dummy you have built yourself, such as `islamophobia_high` in @sec-erklaerung, should show readable values in `frequency()` and `crosstab()` instead of bare zeros and ones:

```{r val-labels-set, eval=FALSE}
allbus <- val_labels(allbus, islamophobia_high = c("low" = 0, "high" = 1))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**Caution: `val_labels()` replaces existing labels.** By default, `val_labels()` discards all existing value labels of the variable. For a newly built variable this does not matter. For an ALLBUS variable, however, the labels of the missing codes disappear as well: after `val_labels(allbus, mm01 = c("completely disagree" = 1, "completely agree" = 7))`, `frequency(mm01)` no longer shows `NAP: SPLIT` next to `-11`. If you only want to change or add individual labels, set `.add = TRUE`. All other labels are then kept:

```{r val-labels-add, eval=FALSE}
allbus <- val_labels(allbus, mm01 = c("completely disagree" = 1, "completely agree" = 7), .add = TRUE)
```

`val_labels(allbus, mm01 = NULL)` removes all value labels of a variable.
:::

## Declaring missing values with `na_frequencies()`, `set_na()` and `drop_na()` {#sec-fehlende-werte}

Missing values are normal in social research. Nobody answers every question in a survey: some people skip individual items, some simply do not know, and some are never asked certain questions because of a split design. And some answers were there originally but were lost through a data error.

GESIS therefore distinguishes many kinds of missing values in ALLBUS and codes them with distinct negative numbers. ALLBUS 2023 has 17 different codes. Four of them occur in the six items of our Islamophobia scale (`mm01` to `mm06`):

| Code  | Meaning                                           |
| ----: | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `-42` | DATA ERROR: MR (multiple responses)               |
| `-11` | NAP: SPLIT (not applicable / split module)        |
| `-9`  | NO ANSWER                                         |
| `-8`  | DO NOT KNOW                                       |

Other variables have further codes, such as `-10` NAP: SCREENED OUT (question skipped after a filter question), `-15` NAP: MODE (not asked in this survey mode), `-7` REFUSED, `-32` CANNOT BE GENERATED (for `age`) or `-33` CANNOT BE CODED and `-41` DATA ERROR (for the school-leaving certificate, `educ`). `na_frequencies()` (see below) shows you which codes a particular variable has.

The distinction matters substantively. A “don't know” is methodologically different from a refused answer, and a “not applicable” (the person was never asked the question) is different again from a genuine data error. If you treat these codes as ordinary numbers, which is what happens when you simply include them in a mean, your results are worthless: an “average” life satisfaction of `-3.4` is obviously nonsense.

After the import step, these codes are stored in `allbus` as **tagged NAs**. “Tagged” means that they count as `NA` (missing) in calculations, but in the background they keep the information about which type of missing value they are. So you can still tell them apart later, for example to show how many people chose “don't know”.

In ALLBUS, some item batteries are put to only part of the sample (split design); respondents who are not shown them get the code `-11` (NAP: SPLIT). This applies in particular to the `mm` items of our Islamophobia scale: about 1650 respondents, just under a third, did not see them. The valid N per item is therefore about 3300–3450 rather than 5246. This is intended and belongs in the methods section.

`na_frequencies()` shows you how many cases each missing code has in a particular variable:

```{r na-freq-demo}
na_frequencies(allbus$mm01)
```

You see in one call how many cases fall under each code. This is useful before you decide whether to keep certain codes as regular values or to treat them as missing for good.

In @fig-missing-codes, each of these gaps is an empty brick with a sticker: the brick is empty because there is no valid value, and the sticker gives the reason. The tags `g`, `l`, `n` and `o` distinguish the four codes within `mm01`. Because the import step gives each of the 17 codes its own tag, a code has the same tag in every variable (for `mm05`, NAP: SPLIT also has the tag `l`). The largest block, 1647 cases with NAP: SPLIT, comes from the split design: these respondents were not asked any of the six `mm` items.

![The four missing codes of `mm01` from `na_frequencies()`. On the right, a diagram of the split design: just under a third of the respondents were not shown the `mm` items.](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-missing-codes.svg){#fig-missing-codes .lightbox fig-alt="At the top the call na_frequencies(allbus$mm01). Below it four rows with the columns code, label, n and tag, each with an empty dashed brick and a yellow sticker: -42 DATA ERROR: MR, n 2, NA(g); -11 NAP: SPLIT, n 1647, NA(l), outlined in orange; -9 NO ANSWER, n 73, NA(n); -8 DO NOT KNOW, n 123, NA(o). On the right under SPLIT DESIGN six towers mm01 to mm06, each with two blue bricks and one empty brick; the row of empty bricks is outlined in orange. Below: two thirds: questions asked; just under a third: NAP: SPLIT."}

**Stop and think.** What does `sum(is.na(allbus$mm01))` return?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
```{r missing-codes-loesung}
sum(is.na(allbus$mm01))
```

`is.na()` only checks whether a value is missing. All four codes therefore count as `NA`, whatever the reason: 2 + 1647 + 73 + 123 = 1845. `na_frequencies()` shows how the gaps are distributed across the reasons.
:::

If you want certain valid codes to count as missing in your analysis, you declare them with `set_na()`. An example: for the school-leaving certificate, `educ`, the categories OTHER SCHOOL CERTIF. (code 6) and STILL AT SCHOOL (code 7) cannot be assigned to any level of education. You give the variable as the name and the codes as values, `variable = c(code1, code2)`:

```{r set-na-demo}
#| message: true
allbus |>
  set_na(educ = c(6, 7), verbose = TRUE) |>
  frequency(educ)
```

With `verbose = TRUE`, mariposa tells you how many values became `NA`, so you can check the step. The two codes then appear with their labels in the missing block of the frequency table: they no longer count as valid, but they can still be told apart as separate missing types. If you leave out the variable name (`set_na(-99)`), the code applies to all numeric variables. The import step at the start of this chapter uses `set_na()` in this way for the 17 ALLBUS codes.

@fig-set-na shows what happens: the bricks with 6 and 7 lose their value and become empty, but their stickers stay. This is why both codes appear in the missing block of the output, with 18 and 26 cases. The number of valid cases falls by these 44 to 5093.

![`set_na()` declares the valid codes 6 and 7 of `educ` as missing values. The bricks become empty, the stickers stay.](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-set-na.svg){#fig-set-na .lightbox fig-alt="On the left under VALID two blue bricks: 6 with the sticker OTHER SCHOOL CERTIF. and 7 with the sticker STILL AT SCHOOL. Above them the call set_na(educ = c(6, 7)) as code bricks. Green arrows lead to the right under MISSING to two empty dashed bricks with the same stickers, next to them N 18 and 26. Below, the output # total N=5246 valid N=5093 and 18 + 26 = 44 fewer valid values."}

`drop_na()` (from tidyr) removes cases with `NA`:

```{r drop-na}
allbus |>
  select(mm01, mm02, mm03) |>
  drop_na() |>
  nrow()
```

`drop_na()` keeps only the rows without a gap (@fig-drop-na). In row 53, only `mm02` is missing (NO ANSWER); the row is still dropped entirely, together with its valid answers 1 and 4. Of the 5246 rows, 3285 remain. In 1739 of the 1961 rows that are dropped, all three values are missing, mostly because of the split design; in the remaining 222, one or two values are missing.

![`drop_na()` removes every row in which at least one value is missing. Row 53 is dropped together with its valid values 1 and 4 (grey).](Bilder/figuren/en/k04-drop-na.svg){#fig-drop-na .lightbox fig-alt="On the left three towers mm01, mm02 and mm03 with the rows 1, 2 and 53. Row 1: 5, 3 and 4. Row 2: three empty dashed bricks. After an ellipsis, row 53, outlined in orange and labelled one gap: 1 and 4 in grey, with an empty brick between them. A green arrow drop_na() leads to the same three towers with only the row 5, 3, 4, below it an ellipsis. Below, the code allbus |> select(mm01, mm02, mm03) |> drop_na() |> nrow() and the output [1] 3285."}

This approach is called **listwise deletion**: a case is dropped as soon as one of the selected variables is `NA`. If you call `drop_na()` in a large pipeline with many variables, your number of cases can shrink drastically. So apply `drop_na()` only to the variables you really need.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Background: MCAR, MAR, MNAR

The methods literature distinguishes three missing-data mechanisms: missing completely at random (MCAR: random, no bias), missing at random (MAR: random conditional on observed variables, can be corrected by modelling) and missing not at random (MNAR: systematic, hard to correct). In survey data such as ALLBUS, MAR is the usual case; simple listwise deletion (`drop_na()`) is then a conservative but transparent way of dealing with it. Imputation methods (for example `mice`) are the next step, but they go beyond an introductory book.
:::

## If something looks strange: a diagnostic cheat sheet {-}

The most common problems beginners have with data import have three causes. The table gives a diagnosis for each:

| Symptom                                                    | Likely cause                                         | Diagnosis                                      |
| :--------------------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------- |
| `mean(allbus$age)` gives strange values (e.g. negative)     | missing codes (-9, -42, …) included as regular numbers | `na_frequencies(allbus$age)`                 |
| plot axis shows numbers (`1`, `2`) instead of labels         | variable is still `<haven_labelled>`, not a factor   | `allbus |> to_label(var)`                      |
| number of cases after `filter()` much smaller than expected | `NA` values are excluded automatically               | `sum(is.na(allbus$var))`                       |

These three cover about 80% of all “why doesn't this work?” moments.

::: {.callout-note}
**Research journal: Where your mini study stands.** You have imported ALLBUS 2023 and have the tools to find your way through 579 variables. You know what lies behind `mm01` to `mm06` (the six Islamophobia items), you know the GESIS missing codes, and you can put together your analysis subset. Next, in @sec-datentransformation, you turn the raw items into two scales: Islamophobia and populism.
:::

## Exercises {-}

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1 · Finding variables · Reproduction"}
You want to build a scale on trust in institutions, but you do not know the variable names by heart. Use `find_var()` to find (a) all variables with “trust” in the label and (b) all variables whose name starts with `st`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r ex1-kap4-loesung, eval=FALSE}
allbus |> find_var("trust", search = "label")
allbus |> find_var("^st", search = "name")
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2 · Codebook of the political trust items · Reproduction"}
Create a `codebook()` for the items `pt01` to `pt08` (trust in various institutions). Look at the labels and value labels. *Tip: there is no item `pt05` in ALLBUS 2023; the range `pt01:pt08` simply selects all columns that lie between them in the dataset.*
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r ex2-kap4-loesung, eval=FALSE}
allbus |>
  codebook(pt01:pt08)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 3 · Building an analysis subset · Transfer"}
Create a dataset `analysis` that contains only the variables needed for the mini study (`mm01:mm06`, `pa29:pa35`, `eastwest`, `sex`, `age`, `educ`, `wghtpew`) and only cases in which at least five of the six `mm` items are valid. *Tip: use `rowSums(!is.na(across(mm01:mm06))) >= 5` as the filter condition.*
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r ex3-kap4-loesung, eval=FALSE}
analysis <- allbus |>
  select(mm01:mm06, pa29:pa35, eastwest, sex, age, educ, wghtpew) |>
  filter(rowSums(!is.na(across(mm01:mm06))) >= 5)
nrow(analysis)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 4 · Your own research question · Mini research question"}
Choose a topic in political science or sociology that interests you (migration, climate, gender roles, …). Use `find_var()` to find two or three variables in ALLBUS 2023 that could shed light on your question. Create a `codebook()` for your selection. Describe in two or three sentences what you would investigate and which variable could serve as the independent and which as the dependent variable.

*There is no model solution here. The exercise is about finding and understanding variables.*
:::

## What you know now {-}

- You import SPSS data with `read_spss()` and keep the variable and value labels.
- You find variables by name or label with `find_var()` and create detailed codebooks with `codebook()`.
- You select variables and cases with `select()`, `filter()` and `arrange()`, and reorder them with `relocate()`.
- You understand the `<haven_labelled>` type and convert it to a factor or a number when needed.
- You read and set variable and value labels with `var_label()` and `val_labels()`.
- You recognise the ALLBUS missing codes, check them with `na_frequencies()` and exclude cases deliberately.

In the next chapter (@sec-datentransformation) you learn how to build the two scales of the mini study from these raw variables: Islamophobia and populism.
